title: Tsunami_Kaiten_Incident_Response_Scenario_3db
description: Investigate and respond to a potential Tsunami/Kaiten malware incident involving suspicious network activity and unauthorized file transfers.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target system has exhibited unusual network activity, including unauthorized connections to external IRC servers and suspicious file transfers. Your task is to investigate and respond to this potential security incident involving the Tsunami/Kaiten malware. Tsunami/Kaiten is a malware family known for creating backdoors and establishing command-and-control (C2) communication through IRC channels. You will need to identify specific ports, services, and file transfer activities as part of your investigation. Tsunami/Kaiten malware can cause significant damage by providing unauthorized access to systems, exfiltrating sensitive data, and maintaining persistence on compromised systems.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system is named `target` and has the IP address `192.168.50.5`. To proceed, enter the word 'start' in the provided input field.
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Network Connections
levels.content: Investigate the suspicious network connections on the target system. Identify and document any unauthorized or suspicious network connections.
levels.solution: Check the network connections and listening ports on the target system using the command `netstat -tuln`. The suspicious port `4444` used for Tsunami/Kaiten C2 communication should be identified.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Network connections can be investigated using various commands. Start by identifying all active network connections and listening ports.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `netstat -tuln` to list all network connections and listening ports. Look for any unusual or unauthorized ports.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Specifically, check for port `4444`, which is known to be used for Tsunami/Kaiten command-and-control (C2) communication in this scenario.

levels.title: Analyze Systemd Services
levels.content: Analyze the systemd services on the target system to identify any suspicious or unauthorized services. Determine if any unauthorized services are running that could be related to the suspicious network activity.
levels.solution: List all systemd services using the command `systemctl list-units --type=service`. Check for any services that look suspicious or unauthorized. The suspicious service `tsunami-kaiten-c2.service` should be identified.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Systemd services can be listed and investigated using specific commands. Start by identifying all active systemd services.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all systemd services. Look for any services that are not part of the standard system configuration.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Specifically, check for the service `tsunami-kaiten-c2.service`, which is known to be suspicious in this scenario.

levels.title: Investigate File Transfers
levels.content: Investigate the file transfers between the target system and the next-target system. Determine if any unauthorized file transfers are occurring between the target system and the next-target system.
levels.solution: Check the logs and systemd services related to file transfers using the command `journalctl -u tsunami-kaiten-file-transfer.service`. The service `tsunami-kaiten-file-transfer.service` responsible for the file transfers should be identified.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: File transfers can be investigated by checking logs and systemd services. Start by identifying services related to file transfers.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the command `journalctl -u tsunami-kaiten-file-transfer.service` to check the logs related to the `tsunami-kaiten-file-transfer.service`. Look for any indications of file transfers.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Specifically, check for the service `tsunami-kaiten-file-transfer.service`, which is known to be responsible for unauthorized file transfers in this scenario.
